item.title: Helm Chart Values
item.description:
The layer5-cloud chart installs the Layer5 Cloud server and, as subcharts from the Ory repository, Kratos and Hydra. The defaults below are those of chart version 0.2.0, which ships with Layer5 Cloud v1.0.278. Run helm show values layer5/layer5-cloud to print the defaults of the version you install. For the install procedure, see Deploy Layer5 Cloud.

How values reach the server 🔗

The chart writes env.* values into one ConfigMap and one Secret, and the server pod reads both as environment variables. Sensitive values go to the Secret. Any change to either rolls the server pods, because the pod template carries a checksum of both.

item.title: Identity Services
item.description:
A self-hosted deployment is its own identity provider. Ory Kratos owns user accounts and sign-in, Ory Hydra issues OAuth2 tokens, and the Layer5 Cloud server connects the two to organizations, teams, and roles. Users can sign up with an email address and password, or with Google or GitHub. For how identity fits together as a concept, see Identity and Security.

What the chart configures by default 🔗

Capability Default
Password sign-in On. Minimum 8 characters, checked against known-breached passwords, and rejected when too similar to the account identifier.
Email verification Required before a password sign-in succeeds. Delivered as a code.
Account recovery On, delivered as a code.
Social sign-in Google and GitHub are enabled but have no credentials until you add them.
Login flow lifespan A started sign-in must finish within 12 hours (720m).
Recovery and verification flow lifespan A recovery or verification request stays valid for 30 days (720h).
Registration flow lifespan A started sign-up must finish within 24 hours.
Session lifespan Not set by the chart. Kratos applies its own default. See Sessions.
Access tokens JWT, valid 24 hours. Refresh tokens are valid 1000 hours, ID tokens 1 hour, and authorization codes 1 hour.

Change any of these through the kratos.kratos.config and hydra.hydra.config values. Both are passed to the Ory services unchanged, so the Kratos and Hydra configuration references apply.

item.title: Plan a Deployment
item.description:
Layer5 Cloud starts with unsafe placeholder values for every secret and with localhost for every URL. Settle the decisions below first, so the install is a single helm install with a complete values file.

Decisions to make 🔗

Decision What to settle Where it is configured
Database A PostgreSQL server that hosts three databases: meshery, kratos, and hydra. env.db, env.kratosdb, env.hydradb, and the subchart dsn values
Hostname and TLS One public hostname, a certificate for it, and the scheme (https). ingress.*, env.serverbaseurl, env.serverHost, env.proto
Secrets Replace every placeholder before first start. See Secrets to generate. env.*, kratos.*, hydra.*
Identity providers The Google and GitHub OAuth applications that act as the default sign-in providers. See Identity Services. env.providerOrg*
Mail A relay on a public address that offers STARTTLS (or implicit TLS on 465), and how identity mail leaves. See Mail. smtp.*, Kratos courier values
First administrator The Provider Admin account and the provider organization. See Provider initialization. env.initConfig
Network paths What must be reachable between components and from users. See Networking. Ingress, network policy, egress rules
Observability Where logs and traces go. See Monitoring. env.loglevel, env.otelConfig

Database 🔗

Layer5 Cloud creates and migrates its own schema. The server applies migrations every time it starts, and exits if a migration fails, so give the database user the rights to create tables and the uuid-ossp extension in the public schema of the meshery database. Kratos and Hydra run their own migrations when the chart’s automigration setting is on, which is the default.

item.title: Deploy Layer5 Cloud
item.description:
This guide installs the layer5-cloud chart, which deploys the Layer5 Cloud server together with Kratos and Hydra. It assumes you have made the decisions in Plan a Deployment. The commands use the release name layer5-cloud in the namespace layer5-cloud.

Prerequisites 🔗

  • A Kubernetes cluster and Helm 3.
  • An ingress controller that supports WebSocket upgrades, and a TLS certificate for your hostname.
  • A PostgreSQL server you can create databases on.
  • An SMTP relay that satisfies the mail constraints, or the decision to run without mail.
  • The OAuth applications for Google and GitHub, if you offer social sign-in.

Install 🔗

1. Prepare the database 🔗

Create one role and three databases on your PostgreSQL server, then create the uuid-ossp extension in the meshery database. The server creates the schema itself.

item.title: Networking
item.description:
Plan these network paths before you deploy. Most are ordinary HTTPS traffic through your ingress. Real-time co-editing is the exception: it connects browsers directly to each other, and the deployment only introduces them.

Required network paths 🔗

From To Protocol Purpose
Browsers, Meshery Servers, API clients Ingress, public hostname HTTPS UI, API, sign-in (/kratos), and OAuth2 (/hydra)
Browsers Ingress, /collaboration WebSocket over HTTPS Co-editing signaling
Layer5 Cloud server Kratos and Hydra services HTTP, in cluster Account and token operations. Default ports: Kratos public 9010 and admin 9011, Hydra public 4444 and admin 4445
Kratos Layer5 Cloud server HTTP, in cluster Registration hooks, and identity mail when the HTTP courier is selected
Layer5 Cloud server, Kratos, Hydra PostgreSQL TCP 5432 Databases meshery, kratos, hydra
Layer5 Cloud server SMTP relay SMTP on 25, 465, 587, or 2525 Mail. The relay must resolve to a public address
Layer5 Cloud server Webhook receivers HTTPS Optional webhooks
Layer5 Cloud server OpenTelemetry collector OTLP gRPC Optional traces
Browsers Public STUN and TURN hosts UDP and TCP Direct connections between co-editing browsers

The ingress must support WebSocket upgrades. A controller or load balancer that closes idle connections shorter than the signaling keep-alive (below) disconnects users from their co-editing session.

item.title: Provider Initialization
item.description:
A new deployment has no users, so nobody can sign in to administer it. Provider initialization solves that: when the server starts with INIT_CONFIG set, it creates the provider organization and its first Provider Admin. From that account, you create organizations, assign roles, and manage the deployment. See Roles and Permissions for what a Provider Admin can do.

Format 🔗

INIT_CONFIG holds a YAML document. In Helm, set it as a multiline string in env.initConfig, or load it from a file with --set-file env.initConfig=provider-init.yaml.

item.title: Customize Webhooks
item.description:
Layer5 Cloud calls an HTTP endpoint you choose when three things happen: a person asks for help, a Provider Admin decides a signup request, and a person gains Kanvas access. The calls let you route those events into your help desk, your chat, or your onboarding automation. On a self-hosted deployment you set the three endpoints; none is set by default, and an unset webhook does nothing useful.

The three webhooks 🔗

Chart value Fires when Payload
env.webhookHelpAndSupport Someone submits the Help and Support form in Layer5 Cloud, or a support request raised in Kanvas reaches your deployment memberFormOne
env.webhookSignupRequest A Provider Admin approves or denies a signup request signupData and newUser
env.webhookKanvasEntitlement A new user registers, a user completes a first brokered social sign-in, or a role assignment gives a user Kanvas access signupData and newUser

Set the endpoints 🔗

Add the three URLs to your Helm values and upgrade. The values are written into the server’s ConfigMap, so the pods restart when you change them.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
Layer5 Cloud gives you four signals: two health endpoints, structured logs with stable error codes, a set of startup messages that tell you whether the deployment is fully working, and optional OpenTelemetry traces. It does not expose a Prometheus metrics endpoint, so build service-level indicators from ingress and Kubernetes metrics plus the signals below.

Health endpoints 🔗

Endpoint Answers Meaning
GET /healthz 200 with the text Cloud is live The process is running. The chart uses it for the liveness probe.
GET /readyz 200 when ready, 503 before The server finished startup and is serving. The chart uses it for the readiness and startup probes.

Both endpoints are unauthenticated. The startup probe allows 20 failed checks at 10-second intervals, so a slow start gets about 200 seconds before Kubernetes restarts the pod. Database migrations run before the server reports ready, so an upgrade that carries a large migration can approach that limit.

item.title: White-label Layer5 Cloud
item.description:
White-labeling lets the people who use your deployment see your brand, not Layer5’s: your logo and colors in the product, your support and legal links on sign-in pages and in email footers, your domain in the address bar, and your address on the mail they receive. Branding is set per organization, so a provider that hosts many organizations can give each its own identity.

White-labeling is part of the Managed Service Provider capability of the Enterprise plan.

item.title: Troubleshoot Email Delivery
item.description: Layer5 Cloud sends two kinds of mail. Application mail (invitations, notifications, welcome mail) leaves the Layer5 Cloud server, through an organization’s own mail server when one is turned on, and otherwise through the shared mail server you configure in the chart’s smtp values. Identity mail (email verification and account recovery) is produced by Kratos and reaches the same server only when you select the HTTP courier. See Plan a Deployment. This guide helps you find which of those paths is failing and why.

item.title: Self-Hosted Deployments
item.description:
A self-hosted deployment runs the same Layer5 Cloud that Layer5 operates, on infrastructure you control. Your users sign in against your identity services, your organizations and designs live in your database, and Meshery Servers in your network connect to your deployment as their remote provider. Your data stays in your database.

Self-hosting is part of the Enterprise plan.

Identity & Access Management
Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise
Cloud as an IDP Own and control the user accounts of your enterprise members with Cloud your identity provider (IdP). -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included
Support and Deployment
Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise
Managed Service Provider White Label: Customize the appearance and branding of your engineering platform powered by Cloud.

Multi-tenancy: Hierarchical organizations, teams, users and customizable permissioning.		 -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included
Self-hosted Deployment Self-hosted Cloud for on-prem appliances or self-managed cloud tenants. Keep your designs internal to your workplace. Get remote support when you need it. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included

What you deploy 🔗

One Helm chart, layer5-cloud, installs the identity-aware application and its two identity services. You supply the database, the ingress, and the TLS certificate.
